claim: The purpose of blinks is to keep the eyes hydrated and to protect them.
source: The purpose of blinks is to keep the eyes hydrated and to protect them.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about blink function in the abstract.

claim: Blink-induced alterations of visual input are blanked out without jeopardizing the perception of visual continuity.
source: Blinks are rarely noticed by the subject as blink-induced alterations of visual input are blanked out without jeopardizing the perception of visual continuity, features blinks share with saccades.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about blink suppression and visual continuity.

claim: Blinks share features with saccades, including blanking out visual input without jeopardizing perception of visual continuity.
source: Blinks are rarely noticed by the subject as blink-induced alterations of visual input are blanked out without jeopardizing the perception of visual continuity, features blinks share with saccades.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about similarities between blinks and saccades.

claim: The blink-induced disconnection from the visual environment leads to a loss of information.
source: Although not perceived, the blink-induced disconnection from the visual environment leads to a loss of information.
evidence: This is stated as a logical consequence of visual interruption during blinks.

claim: There is a critical need to minimize the loss of visual information during blinks.
source: Therefore there is critical need to minimize it.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional importance of continuous visual information.

claim: A new type of eye movement serves the distinct oculomotor demand of resetting eye torsion.
source: Here we demonstrate evidence for a new type of eye movement serving a distinct oculomotor demand, namely the resetting of eye torsion, likewise inevitably causing a loss of visual information.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The new eye movement for resetting eye torsion inevitably causes a loss of visual information.
source: Here we demonstrate evidence for a new type of eye movement serving a distinct oculomotor demand, namely the resetting of eye torsion, likewise inevitably causing a loss of visual information.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the eye movement interrupting vision.

claim: By integrating the torsion-resetting eye movement into blinks, the inevitable down times of vision associated with each behavior are synchronized and the overall downtime minimized.
source: By integrating this eye movement into blinks, the inevitable down times of vision associated with each of the two behaviors are synchronized and the overall downtime minimized.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by experimental observations of blink-associated resetting movements.

claim: We normally blink around 15 to 20 times per minute.
source: We normally blink around 15 to 20 times per minute to hydrate the eyes and to protect them from potentially harmful agents (Evinger, 1995; Evinger et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Normal visual input is blanked out for approximately 300 milliseconds during blinks.
source: Although normal visual input is blanked out for ~300 milliseconds during blinks, we rarely perceive these gaps due to what is called blink suppression (Bristow et al., 2005; Volkmann et al., 1980; Volkmann, 1986; Manning et al., 1983), the attenuation of visual sensitivity during blinks.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Blink suppression is the attenuation of visual sensitivity during blinks.
source: Although normal visual input is blanked out for ~300 milliseconds during blinks, we rarely perceive these gaps due to what is called blink suppression (Bristow et al., 2005; Volkmann et al., 1980; Volkmann, 1986; Manning et al., 1983), the attenuation of visual sensitivity during blinks.
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations.

claim: Blink suppression is useful to eliminate the visual consequences of eye and lid movements during blinks.
source: This mechanism is useful to eliminate the visual consequences of eye and lid movements during blinks (Ridder and Tomlinson, 1997; Volkmann et al., 1968).
evidence: This is stated as an established function with supporting citations.

claim: Blink suppression comes with the cost of losing the connection to the visual world for the duration of the blink.
source: But it comes with the cost of losing the connection to the visual world for the duration of the blink (VanderWerf et al., 2003; Bour et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as a consequence with supporting citations.

claim: Without compensation, the loss of visual connection during blinks would lead to discontinuous visual perception.
source: Without compensation this loss would lead to a discontinuous visual perception.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of uncompensated visual gaps.

claim: The visual system is able to ensure an illusion of continuity by bridging the perceptual gaps during blinks.
source: However, previous experiments in humans have shown that the visual system is able to ensure an illusion of continuity by bridging the perceptual gaps (Bristow et al., 2005; Shultz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Blink frequency may be temporarily reduced when quick behavioral responses may be demanded.
source: Moreover, in cases quick behavioral responses may be demanded, the blink frequency may be temporarily reduced in order to provide more time for the processing of behaviorally relevant visual information.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about adaptive blink behavior.

claim: During reading, we blink only 4-5 times per minute instead of 15-20 times per minute.
source: For example during reading, we blink only 4–5 instead of 15–20 times per minute (Shultz et al., 2011; Bentivoglio et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Blinks are synchronized with saccades to reduce the down time of the visual system.
source: Another mechanism, reducing the down time of the visual system is the synchronization of blinks with saccades, the latter likewise blanking out vision due to saccadic suppression (Fogarty and Stern, 1989; Zee et al., 1983; Evinger et al., 1991, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Saccades blank out vision due to saccadic suppression.
source: Another mechanism, reducing the down time of the visual system is the synchronization of blinks with saccades, the latter likewise blanking out vision due to saccadic suppression (Fogarty and Stern, 1989; Zee et al., 1983; Evinger et al., 1991, 1984).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Torsional optokinetic nystagmus (tOKN) is one of the oculomotor reflexes that stabilize the visual background.
source: One of these reflexes is the torsional optokinetic nystagmus (tOKN) (Farooq et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Torsional optokinetic nystagmus consists of a slow phase in which the eyes pursue the rotation of the visual stimulus followed by a torsional fast phase in the opposite direction.
source: It consists of a slow phase in which the eyes pursue the rotation of the visual stimulus in order to reduce the slip of its retinal image, followed by a torsional fast phase in the opposite direction.
evidence: This is a description of the tOKN mechanism based on established knowledge.

claim: The slow phase of tOKN aims to reduce the slip of the retinal image.
source: It consists of a slow phase in which the eyes pursue the rotation of the visual stimulus in order to reduce the slip of its retinal image, followed by a torsional fast phase in the opposite direction.
evidence: This is stated as the functional purpose of the slow phase.

claim: The fast phase of tOKN ensures that the eyes stay within the mechanical limits of the plant.
source: The fast phase, generally considered to rely on the brainstem premotor circuitry for saccades (Tozzi et al., 2007), ensures that the eyes stay within the mechanical limits of the plant.
evidence: This is stated as the functional purpose of the fast phase with a supporting citation.

claim: The fast phase of tOKN is generally considered to rely on the brainstem premotor circuitry for saccades.
source: The fast phase, generally considered to rely on the brainstem premotor circuitry for saccades (Tozzi et al., 2007), ensures that the eyes stay within the mechanical limits of the plant.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Rather than combining fast phases with blinks, the oculomotor system deploys a novel type of resetting movement which is qualitatively different from fast phases.
source: Here we report that the overarching goal to optimize visual perception is actually met in a surprisingly different manner. Rather than combining fast phases with blinks, the oculomotor system deploys a novel type of resetting movement which is qualitatively different from fast phases.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: During the 'fixation in darkness' phase I, the mean torsional eye position was taken as reference for eye torsion (zero torsion).
source: The mean torsional eye position during the first phase (fixation in darkness I), when only the central fixation dot was visible, was taken as reference for eye torsion (referred to as zero torsion from now on).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: During the 'fixation in darkness' phase I, eye torsion fluctuated around zero by ± 2 deg.
source: During the 'fixation in darkness' phase I, which lasted for 180 s, the eye torsion fluctuated around zero by ± 2 deg (mean ± std, by averaging the individual means of subjects, calculated as the average of the eye position for the 180 s).
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The eyes followed the torsional flow with a mean velocity of approximately 2.95 ± 2.9 deg/s.
source: The eyes followed the torsional flow with a mean velocity of ~2.95 ± 2.9 deg/s (mean ± std across subjects).
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The slow phase of tOKN was interrupted by fast movements in the opposite direction (fast phases).
source: This following movement, the slow phase of the torsional optokinetic nystagmus (tOKN), was time and again interrupted by fast movements in the opposite direction, corresponding to the fast phases of the tOKN, which aim to move the eyes back towards zero torsion.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The resetting by fast phases was imperfect, resulting in a gradual build-up of torsion in the direction of the optic flow until a plateau of approximately 3-8 deg was reached.
source: This resetting was, however, imperfect as reflected by a gradual build-up in the direction of the optic flow until a plateau of ~3–8 deg was reached.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The build-up of torsion is a consequence of a smaller cumulative amplitude of fast phases compared to the cumulative amplitude of slow phases.
source: This build-up is a consequence of a smaller cumulative amplitude of fast phases as compared to the cumulative amplitude of slow phases.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed data.

claim: During the 'fixation in darkness' phase II, the overall eye torsion slowly drifted back towards zero torsion, usually without fully reaching it.
source: When the optic flow phase had ended, a fixation period of 180 s duration in total darkness followed (fixation in darkness II). During this time the overall eye torsion slowly drifted back towards zero torsion, yet, usually without fully reaching it.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: During the 'optic flow' phases I and II, a change in eye position towards zero torsion was observed associated with each blink.
source: During the 'optic flow' phases I and II, once the eyes showed an optokinetic nystagmus and had gradually reached their respective plateau of up to 8 deg, we observed a change in the eye position towards zero torsion associated with each blink.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The amplitudes of BARMs were in the order of one degree (1.34 ± 1.3 deg).
source: The amplitudes of these BARMs were in the order of one degree (1.34 ± 1.3 deg, mean ± std across subjects).
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data.

claim: In the 'fixation in darkness' phase I, BARMs were less frequent, more variable in direction and smaller (0.6 ± 0.89 deg) compared to optic flow phases.
source: In the 'fixation in darkness' phase I, when only the fixation dot was present and deviations from zero were small, BARMs were also seen, but they were less frequent, more variable in direction and smaller (0.6 ± 0.89 deg, mean ± std, see Figure 2A,D).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data with reference to figures.

claim: In the 'fixation in darkness' phase II, BARMs were much more frequent and of larger amplitude (0.68 ± 0.79 deg) compared to phase I.
source: In the 'fixation in darkness' phase II, however, in which the visual conditions were not different from the 'fixation in darkness' phase I, but the average eye position had not yet fully returned to zero torsion, BARMs were much more frequent and of larger amplitude (0.68 ± 0.79 deg mean ± std, p=0.02, fixation in darkness phase II vs. fixation in darkness phase I, see Figure 2C,F for one of the subjects; for the other subjects see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data with statistical comparison.

claim: The probability and amplitude of BARMs are determined by the deviation of the eyes from zero torsion, regardless of whether an optokinetic stimulus is present.
source: This suggests that the probability and the amplitude of BARMs are determined by the deviation of the eyes from zero torsion, no matter if an optokinetic stimulus is present or not.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations across different phases.

claim: The amplitude of BARMs is linearly correlated with the size of the pre-blink torsional eye position.
source: In accordance with this view, we found the amplitude of BARMs to be linearly correlated with the size of the pre-blink torsional eye position, which is the deviation from zero torsion (see Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data with reference to a figure.

claim: The amplitude of BARMs is not related to the slow phase preceding the blink.
source: In contrast, the amplitude of BARMs was not related to the slow phase preceding the blink, since the amplitude of the slow phase, defined by the difference of the torsional eye position between the onset of the slow phase and the onset of the blink, was not correlated with the amplitude of BARMs (see Figure 3B, for the other subjects see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data with reference to figures.

claim: The absolute torsional eye position matters for BARM amplitude but the latest history of the slow phase does not.
source: In other words, the absolute torsional eye position matters but the latest history of the slow phase does not.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the correlation analyses.

claim: The correlation between BARM amplitude and pre-blink eye position was strongest for the 'optic flow' phases I and II.
source: Although the correlation between the amplitude of BARMs and the pre-blink eye position was strongest for the 'optic flow' phase I and II (see Table 1), in which the optokinetic stimulus was present and the deviation from zero was largest, we found similar relationships also for the 'fixation in darkness' phase I and phase II.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis with reference to a table.

claim: BARMs are a ubiquitous phenomenon not restricted to optic flow stimuli.
source: This supports the view that BARMs are not restricted to optic flow stimuli but that they are a ubiquitous phenomenon.
evidence: This is an inference from observations across different experimental conditions.

claim: The BARM amplitude is not only dependent on the pre-blink torsional eye position but additionally influenced by the average torsional eye position of a phase.
source: This indicates that the BARM amplitude is not only dependent on the pre-blink torsional eye position preceding a single BARM but additionally influenced by the average torsional eye position of a phase.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of constrained ranges of pre-blink eye positions.

claim: There is a gain modulation of the linear relation between pre-blink torsional eye position and BARM amplitude according to superordinate requirements.
source: It suggests a gain modulation of the linear relation between pre-blink torsional eye position and BARM amplitude according to superordinate requirements.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed phase-dependent differences in regression slopes.

claim: The occurrence of BARMs during the 'fixation in darkness' phases I and II argues against BARMs being fast phases coinciding with blinks.
source: Are BARMs, in fact, fast phases coinciding with blinks? The occurrence of BARMs during the 'fixation in darkness' phases I and II argues against this objection.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations in darkness phases.

claim: In the case of fast phases, the preceding slow phase amplitude explains a large part of the amplitude of the following fast phase.
source: In the case of fast phases, the preceding slow phase amplitude, i.e. the difference between the onset and the offset of the slow phase explains a large part of the amplitude of the following fast phase (r = −0.35 ± 0.1 mean ± std. across subjects, Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, mean slope of 0.33).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis with reference to figures.

claim: The torsional eye position at the onset of the fast phase has little if any influence on the size of the fast phase amplitude.
source: On the other hand, the torsional eye position at the onset of the fast phase has little if any influence on the size of the fast phase amplitude (correlations are only weak and inconsistent: significant correlation in 3 out of 5 subjects, r = −0.18 ± 0.09 mean ± std. across subjects, see Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis with reference to figures.

claim: BARMs and fast phases are functionally two distinct entities.
source: We conclude that BARMs and fast phases are functionally two distinct entities (see Figure 3C and F).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential dependencies of BARMs and fast phases on pre-shift eye position and slow phase amplitude.

claim: Four out of five subjects had long lasting blink-associated eye movements composed of two clearly distinct components.
source: Four out of five subjects had long lasting blink-associated eye movements, composed of two clearly distinct components (Ha: 369 ± 54 ms; Mo 316 ± 18 ms; Da 367 ± 13 ms; Ph 372 ± 45 ms mean ± std duration).
evidence: This is an observation from search coil recordings.

claim: The peak of the first component of blink-associated eye movement was about 130 ms from blink onset with an amplitude of about 1.2 degrees.
source: As illustrated in Figure 4 for subject Ha, the peak of the first component was about 130 ms from blink onset (subject Ha: 107 ± 10 ms, mean ± std, all subjects: 127 ± 35 ms) with an amplitude of about 1.2 degree (Ha: 1.6 ± 0.12 deg, all subjects: 1.14 ± 0.47 deg).
evidence: This is a measurement from search coil recordings with reference to a figure.

claim: The torsional dimension of the first component was always directed clockwise (extorsional for the right eye).
source: The torsional dimension of the first component was always directed clockwise. Since the right eye was measured this component corresponds to an extorsional eye movement.
evidence: This is an observation from search coil recordings.

claim: The first component was supplemented by a nasal downward movement compared to the pre-blink position.
source: It was supplemented by a nasal downward movement as compared to the pre-blink position.
evidence: This is an observation from search coil recordings.

claim: The properties of the first component match those previously described for blinks during fixation.
source: These properties match the ones previously described for blinks during fixation (Bour et al., 2000; Bergamin et al., 2002; Straumann et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous research supported by citations.

claim: The first component was found not only in the 'fixation in darkness' phases but also in the 'optic flow' phases.
source: Importantly, we found this first component not only in the 'fixation in darkness' phase I and II, when the subject had to fixate in darkness, but also in the 'optic flow' phase I and II when the optic flow was present.
evidence: This is an observation from search coil recordings.

claim: The profile of the first component did not change significantly between phases.
source: The profile of this first component did not change significantly between phases and, most noteworthy, the direction of it was not changed by the direction of the optic flow, which would be required if it had a compensatory role (see Figure 4).
evidence: This is an observation from search coil recordings with reference to a figure.

claim: The direction of the first component was not changed by the direction of the optic flow.
source: The profile of this first component did not change significantly between phases and, most noteworthy, the direction of it was not changed by the direction of the optic flow, which would be required if it had a compensatory role (see Figure 4).
evidence: This is an observation from search coil recordings with reference to a figure.

claim: The torsional amplitude of the first component was larger when the optic flow pointed in the same direction (clockwise) compared to counterclockwise direction.
source: The only relation between the first component's torsional dimension and BARMs was found in 'optic flow' phase I and II, in which the torsional amplitude was larger when the optic flow pointed in the same direction, i.e. clockwise, as compared to the counterclockwise direction.
evidence: This is an observation from search coil recordings.

claim: There was a negative correlation between the amplitude of the first component and the amplitude of BARMs (r = −0.43, p=0.0001).
source: This was reflected by a negative correlation between the amplitude of the first component and the amplitude of BARMs (r = −0.43, p=0.0001, based on the four subjects with two components).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis.

claim: The first component cannot account for the compensatory action of BARMs.
source: In other words, the tiny influence of the optic flow on the first component was congruent with the optic flow direction. For this reason it cannot account for the compensatory action of BARMs.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed direction of the first component relative to optic flow.

claim: The torsional direction of the second component depended on the direction of the optic flow and was always directed opposite to the optic flow.
source: Of decisive importance is the fact that the torsional direction of the second component depended on the direction of the optic flow. As expected for a compensatory mechanism, it was always directed opposite to the optic flow.
evidence: This is an observation from search coil recordings.

claim: The amplitude of the torsional component of the second component was larger during optic flow phases compared to non-optic flow phases.
source: Moreover, the amplitude of the torsional component was larger during optic flow phases, when there was more need for resetting, as compared to non-optic flow phases.
evidence: This is an observation from search coil recordings.

claim: The torsional amplitude of the second component correlated with the amplitude of BARMs measured by video records.
source: As a matter of fact, the torsional amplitude of the second component correlated with the amplitude of BARMs, the latter measured as in the video records by comparing pre- and post-blink eye torsion. This correlation could be seen for all phases and subjects (fixation in darkness phase I: r = 0.63, p<0.05; optic flow phase I and II: r = 0.96, p<0.05; fixation in darkness phase II: r = 0.87, p<0.05, based on pooled data from four out of five subjects).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis comparing search coil and video data.

claim: No consistent relationships were found between the amplitude of BARMs and the horizontal and vertical eye movements accompanying the blink.
source: Finally, we found no consistent relationships between the amplitude of BARMs and the horizontal and vertical eye movements accompanying the blink.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis.

claim: The second component makes the decisive contribution to the BARMs documented by video eye tracking.
source: In sum, it is the second component, which makes the decisive contribution to the BARMs documented by video eye tracking.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the correlation between the second component and BARMs.

claim: The second component acts independently of accompanying vertical and horizontal eye movements.
source: Moreover, the second component acts independently of accompanying vertical and horizontal eye movements.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of correlation between BARM amplitude and horizontal/vertical movements.

claim: An eye movement qualifies as a saccade if the relationship between its amplitude and peak velocity satisfies the main sequence relationship.
source: From a kinematic point of view, an eye movement qualifies as a saccade if the relationship between its amplitude and peak velocity satisfies the main sequence relationship, first established for visually guided saccades [Bahill et al., (1975)].
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Fast phases of tOKN showed the expected monotonic, almost linear growth of peak velocity with amplitude.
source: A plot of the fast phases of the tOKN in the 'optic flow' phases I and II showed the expected monotonic, almost linear growth of peak velocity with amplitude (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an observation from kinematic analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: The first component of blink-associated eye movements did not show a consistent dependency of peak velocity on amplitude for all subjects.
source: While the first component of blink-associated eye movements recorded with search coils did - as expected - not show a consistent dependency of peak velocity on amplitude for all subjects, the second component (=BARM) exhibited the typical relationship of a saccadic eye movement not that different from that of fast phases although the regression line was significantly shifted to slower velocities (p<0.05 for all subjects) (see Materials and methods, and Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from kinematic analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: The second component (BARM) exhibited the typical relationship of a saccadic eye movement with the regression line significantly shifted to slower velocities compared to fast phases.
source: While the first component of blink-associated eye movements recorded with search coils did - as expected - not show a consistent dependency of peak velocity on amplitude for all subjects, the second component (=BARM) exhibited the typical relationship of a saccadic eye movement not that different from that of fast phases although the regression line was significantly shifted to slower velocities (p<0.05 for all subjects) (see Materials and methods, and Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from kinematic analysis with statistical comparison and reference to a figure.

claim: In kinematic terms, BARMs are a special type of saccade that can be distinguished from fast phases because of their very different main sequence profile.
source: Hence, in kinematic terms BARMs are a special type of saccade that can be distinguished from fast phases because of their very different main sequence profile.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the kinematic analysis.

claim: The lack of optic flow input during blinks cannot explain the occurrence of BARMs.
source: Although we obtained significant correlations between the size of the torsional eye shift during blanking and the eye torsion before blanking in 4 out of 5 subjects, the slopes of the linear regressions were almost zero in all of five subjects. Thus, the lack of optic flow input during blinks cannot explain the occurrence of BARMs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulated blink experiment.

claim: No correlation was found between blink duration and the amplitude of BARMs for true or simulated blinks.
source: In line with this conclusion, we did not find any correlation between blink duration and the amplitude of BARMs, neither for true nor for simulated blinks, a relationship one might have expected if it was the lack of optic flow that drove the eye back to zero torsion (see Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis with reference to figures.

claim: Measurements by video-oculography did not exhibit any consistent correlation between blink-associated eye position shifts and pre-blink eye positions for horizontal or vertical dimensions when considering each experimental phase and subject separately.
source: When considering each experimental phase and subject separately, measurements by video-oculography did not exhibit any consistent correlation between blink-associated eye position shifts and pre-blink eye positions, neither for the horizontal nor for the vertical dimension.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of video-oculography data.

claim: Search coil recordings consistently found a significant correlation between eye position shifts and pre-blink eye positions for horizontal, vertical, and torsional dimensions.
source: Therefore, we also analyzed eye data obtained with the search coil technique, offering a much higher spatial resolution (see Materials and methods for details). As a result, we now consistently found a significant correlation between eye position shifts and pre-blink eye positions for both, horizontal and vertical dimensions as well as for the torsional dimension (see Figure 7).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of search coil data with reference to a figure.

claim: BARMs are sensitive enough to compensate for small vertical deviations of less than 1 deg.
source: This is remarkable in view of the small vertical deviations of less than 1 deg. BARMs are obviously sensitive enough to compensate for them.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of vertical BARMs in response to small deviations.

claim: BARMs help to avoid the accumulation of excessive eye torsion building up in response to torsional optic flow by resetting the torsional deviation.
source: In this study we have demonstrated the existence of a distinct, hitherto unknown type of eye movement. It helps to avoid the accumulation of excessive eye torsion, building up in response to torsional optic flow by time and again resetting the torsional deviation.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: BARMs are a key element of a motor synergy in which they are yoked with eye blinks.
source: This new eye movement is a key element of a motor synergy in which it is yoked with eye blinks, which is why we refer to it as blink-associated resetting eye movement (BARM).
evidence: This is a characterization of the main finding.

claim: The horizontal and vertical movement components complementing the torsional resetting response are qualitatively different from those of the fast phases of the tOKN.
source: The horizontal and vertical movement components complementing the torsional resetting response are qualitatively different from those of the fast phases of the tOKN.
evidence: This is stated as a distinguishing feature of BARMs.

claim: The amplitude of BARMs is correlated with the pre-blink torsional eye position but not with the amplitude of the preceding slow phase component of the tOKN, a relationship which is exactly opposite to the fast phases of the OKN.
source: The amplitude of BARMs is correlated with the pre-blink torsional eye position but not with the amplitude of the preceding slow phase component of the tOKN, a relationship, which is exactly opposite to the fast phases of the OKN as also reported before (Watanabe et al., 1994; Waddington and Harris, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a distinguishing feature with supporting citations.

claim: BARMs differ in the main sequence relationship from tOKN fast phases.
source: BARMs differ in the main sequence relationship from tOKN fast phases.
evidence: This is stated as a distinguishing feature based on kinematic analysis.

claim: BARMs are observed in the absence of an optokinetic stimulus in case significant amounts of eye torsion may have arisen spontaneously.
source: BARMs are also observed in the absence of an optokinetic stimulus in case significant amounts of eye torsion may have arisen spontaneously.
evidence: This is stated as a distinguishing feature based on observations in darkness phases.

claim: Similar blink-associated resetting eye movements are deployed to reset eye deviations from straight ahead in the vertical and horizontal dimension.
source: Similar blink-associated resetting eye movements are deployed to reset eye deviations from straight ahead in the vertical and horizontal dimension.
evidence: This is stated as a generalization based on search coil data.

claim: BARMs are a distinct type of eye movement that is a ubiquitous partner of eye blinks.
source: In sum, we suggest that BARMs are a distinct type of eye movement that is a ubiquitous partner of eye blinks.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: BARMs were found independent of the specific condition that had led to eye torsion, consistently across subjects and independent of the two eye movement recording methods used.
source: As said before, BARMs were found independent of the specific condition that had led to eye torsion, consistently across subjects and independent of the two eye movement recording methods we used, video eye tracking and search coil recordings.
evidence: This is a summary of the robustness of the findings.

claim: Video eye tracking has the advantage of avoiding any interaction with the eye and the eye lids.
source: Video eye tracking has the advantage of avoiding any interaction with the eye and the eye lids.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological consideration.

claim: Video eye tracking does not provide information for the time the eyes are covered by the eye lids.
source: On the other hand, it does not provide information for the time the eyes are covered by the eye lids.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of video eye tracking.

claim: Search coil recordings allowed documentation of a sequence of two movement components during blinks.
source: Complementary search coil recordings allowed us to fill this gap and to document a sequence of two movement components.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of search coil recordings.

claim: The first component does not account for the properties of BARMs, but the second one does.
source: Whereas the first one does not account for the properties of BARMs, the second one does.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of the two components.

claim: The congruency of the overall amount of resetting documented with video eye tracking and search coil recordings argues against the second component being an artifact of the search coil recording technique.
source: Yet, the congruency of the overall amount of resetting documented with video eye tracking and search coil recordings clearly speaks against this concern.
evidence: This is an argument against a potential methodological artifact.

claim: Although BARMs reset eye torsion, this resetting is not complete if torsion is induced by torsional optic flow.
source: Firstly, although BARMs reset eye torsion, this resetting is not complete if torsion is induced by torsional optic flow.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Torsional deviations observed in the absence of torsional optic flow show more complete resetting to zero by BARMs.
source: This stands in contrast to torsional deviations observed in the absence of torsional optic flow where we observed more BARMs leading the eyes back to zero.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The building up of a torsion plateau in reaction to steady state torsional optic flow might reflect an adaptive shift of the subjective vertical.
source: Actually it is tempting to speculate that the building up of a torsion plateau in reaction to the exposure to steady state torsional optic flow might reflect an adaptive shift of the subjective vertical.
evidence: This is stated as speculation about the mechanism.

claim: BARMs would be driven by the deviation from the adapted torsional zero rather than from a baseline zero.
source: Interpreted this way, BARMs would not be driven by the deviation of the eyes from a baseline zero but by the deviation from the adapted torsional zero (Thilo and Gresty, 2002; Ibbotson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as speculation with supporting citations.

claim: The influence of pre-blink eye torsion on BARM amplitude depends on context and history.
source: The second aspect is that the influence of the level of pre-blink eye torsion on the amplitude of BARMs depends on context and history.
evidence: This is an inference from the phase-dependent differences in regression slopes.

claim: The modulation of the slope of the BARM-amplitude vs. pre-blink eye torsion relationship helps to counteract the accumulation of eye torsion in the presence of strong torsional optic flow.
source: This modulation of the slope is actually quite useful as it helps to counteract the accumulation of eye torsion in the presence of strong torsional optic flow.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the observed modulation.

claim: The evidence available clearly argues for active control of BARMs rather than a biomechanical artifact.
source: Hence, the evidence available clearly argues for active control of BARMs rather than a biomechanical artifact.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the properties of BARMs.

claim: BARMs are an active process linked to blinks rather than being elicited by an interruption of vision.
source: It is an active process linked to blinks rather than being elicited by an interruption of vision as indicated by control experiments in which we simulated the blink-associated interruption of the visual input.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulated blink experiment.

claim: The first component corresponds to the classical blink-associated eye movement which is directed nasally, downward and extorsional.
source: The first component corresponds to the classical blink-associated eye movement which is directed nasally, downward and extorsional - a reflex that has been suggested to support the hydration and protection of the eye (Evinger et al., 1991; Evinger, 1995).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The classical blink-associated eye movement is a reflex that has been suggested to support the hydration and protection of the eye.
source: The first component corresponds to the classical blink-associated eye movement which is directed nasally, downward and extorsional - a reflex that has been suggested to support the hydration and protection of the eye (Evinger et al., 1991; Evinger, 1995).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The independence of the two components argues that the first component is a rigid blink-specific eye movement not related to other types of oculomotor behavior serving vision.
source: The independence of the two components is documented by the consistent direction of the first independent of the resetting direction of torsion, and the absence of the consistent amplitude vs. velocity relationship that characterizes the second component, an independence that argues that the latter is a rigid blink-specific eye movement that is not related to other types of oculomotor behavior serving vision.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed independence of the two components.

claim: Previous work on search coil recordings of blink-associated eye movements had noted the occurrence of a second component but did not address its function.
source: Although previous work on search coil recordings of blink-associated eye movements had noted the occurrence of a second component, it did not address its function (Bergamin et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Changes in saccade velocity have been observed in response to a wide variety of conditions.
source: Changes in saccade velocity have actually been observed in response to a wide variety of conditions (Prsa et al., 2010; Shadmehr, 2010).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Saccades which coincide with blinks have latencies and kinematics that differ from those of non-blink-associated saccades.
source: Most importantly, it is well-known that saccades which coincide with blinks have latencies and kinematics that differ from those of non-blink-associated saccades (Goossens and Van Opstal, 2000; Powers et al., 2013; Rottach et al., 1998; Rambold et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Patients suffering from pathology of the brainstem premotor circuits for saccades exhibit slow saccades which may be faster if associated with a blink.
source: Unlike healthy subjects, these patients exhibit slow saccades which may be faster if they are associated with a blink.
evidence: This is stated as clinical observation.

claim: In extreme cases of brainstem pathology, only blink-associated saccades may be left while others are lacking completely.
source: Actually in extreme cases only blink-associated saccades may be left, while others are lacking completely (Zee et al., 1983).
evidence: This is stated as clinical observation with a supporting citation.

claim: The putative blink-associated saccades in clinical cases of brainstem pathology could actually be BARMs.
source: Rather than assuming a facilitatory influence of blink-related signals on a run-down saccade generator, a more parsimonious interpretation could be that the putative blink-associated saccades in these clinical case are actually BARMs, still possible because the underlying circuitry may have been spared by the pathology.
evidence: This is stated as speculation about clinical observations.

claim: Blink-associated oscillations observed in patients with neurodegenerative brainstem disease with normal saccades might be a manifestation of a degenerated BARM generator sparing the saccade generator.
source: On the other hand, the blink-associated oscillations that have been observed in patients suffering from neurodegenerative brainstem disease with normal saccades (Hain et al., 1986) might be a manifestation of a degenerated BARM generator sparing the saccade generator.
evidence: This is stated as speculation with a supporting citation.

claim: The speculative conclusion is the assumption of a far-reaching dissociation of the generators of BARMs and saccades.
source: In other words, the speculative conclusion would be the assumption of a far-reaching dissociation of the generators of BARMs and saccades.
evidence: This is stated as speculation.

claim: Patients suffering from a loss of saccades might train to deploy BARMs more frequently and efficiently.
source: The practical implication of this scenario could be that patients suffering from a loss of saccades might actually train to deploy BARMs more frequently and efficiently.
evidence: This is stated as speculation about potential clinical applications.

claim: Blink-associated resetting eye movements represent a distinct type of eye movement intimately linked to eye blinks that helps keep the deviation from a baseline torsional eye position small, thereby supporting stable spatial vision.
source: In summary, blink-associated resetting eye movements represent a distinct type of eye movement intimately linked to eye blinks, helping the observer to keep the deviation from a baseline torsional eye position small, thereby supporting stable spatial vision.
evidence: This is the summary conclusion of the study.

claim: Preliminary evidence suggests that BARMs may not be restricted to torsion but may help to keep also horizontal and vertical deviations at bay.
source: While we explored the properties of these eye movements primarily in the torsional domain, preliminary evidence suggests that they may not be restricted to torsion but may help to keep also horizontal and vertical deviations at bay.
evidence: This is stated as preliminary evidence from the study.

claim: Yoking BARMs with the closure of the eyelids is an ecologically useful synergy that helps to minimize the downtime of vision.
source: Yoking these eye movements with the closure of the eyelids is an ecologically useful synergy that helps to minimize the downtime of vision that is inevitably associated with both.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the synergy.

claim: Each BARM makes a resetting saccade of 50 ms length waivable, resulting in a gain of 15 minutes of uncompromised vision every day.
source: Considering that we blink on average 18 times per minute over 16 hr of wakefulness per day and furthermore that each BARM makes a resetting saccade of 50 ms length waivable, the gain in uncompromised vision is substantial, amounting to 15 mins every day.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Eleven human subjects without known neurological diseases participated in the experiments.
source: Eleven human subjects without known neurological diseases participated in the experiments of this study (3 females, 8 males, age 25–33).
evidence: This describes the study participants.

claim: All subjects had normal or corrected-to-normal visual acuity.
source: All subjects had normal or corrected-to-normal visual acuity and gave written informed consent according to the declaration of Helsinki prior to the experiment.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for subjects.

claim: The study was approved by the institutional ethics committee.
source: The study was approved by the institutional ethics committee.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval.

claim: All experiments were carried out in darkness.
source: All experiments were carried out in darkness.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions.

claim: Subjects sat with their head gently restrained by a chin and forehead rest at a distance of 60 cm from the stimulus display.
source: Subjects sat with their head gently restrained by a chin and forehead rest for the duration of the experiments at a distance of 60 cm from the stimulus display.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: The stimuli were presented on a large frontoparallel tangent screen (160 cm width and 120 cm height, 108 × 90 deg visual angle).
source: The stimuli were presented on a large frontoparallel tangent screen (160 cm width and 120 cm height, 108 × 90 deg visual angle).
evidence: This describes the stimulus presentation setup.

claim: The tOKN stimulus consisted of a random dot pattern rotating around the naso-occipital axis at an angular speed of 30 deg/s.
source: The tOKN stimulus consisted of a random dot pattern (1500 dots, 0.3 deg diameter of each, density 0.55 dot/deg2) rotating around the naso-occipital axis at an angular speed of 30 deg/s, either clockwise or counterclockwise.
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters.

claim: Eye movements were recorded deploying an infrared video eye tracking system with 50 Hz or 100 Hz sampling rate.
source: We recorded eye movements deploying an infrared video eye tracking system (Chronos Eye Tracking System, Chronos Vision GmbH, Berlin, Germany) with 50 Hz or 100 Hz.
evidence: This describes the eye tracking methodology.

claim: The torsional eye position was computed offline using the iris tracking software based on a cross-correlation algorithm.
source: The torsional eye position was computed offline using the iris tracking software of the system (Chronos Vision GmbH) which determines the rotation relative to a reference frame based on a cross-correlation algorithm (Ong and Haslwanter 2010).
evidence: This describes the method for computing torsional eye position with a citation.

claim: Eye blinks were detected by the transient coverage of the pupil leading to omission of several subsequent samples recognized by accompanying infinite values.
source: Eye blinks were detected by the fact that the transient coverage of the pupil led to the omission of several subsequent samples, recognized by accompanying infinite values.
evidence: This describes the method for detecting blinks.

claim: 3D scleral search coils were used in the third experiment measuring high speed movements made during blinks, with data sampled at 200 Hz.
source: 3D scleral search coils from three different vendors were used: Chronos Vision, Berlin, Germany, Skalar from Delft, Netherlands and Universal trading ventures, Cleveland, USA, were used in the third experiment measuring the high speed movements made during blinks. The data were sampled at 200 Hz.
evidence: This describes the search coil methodology.
